title: Marine Corps Harrier Pilot Rescue
description:
Airmen from the 31st and 33rd Rescue Squadrons, along with Japan Air Self-Defense Force personnel, worked together to rescue a Marine pilot after he ejected from his aircraft about 100 nautical miles off the coast of Okinawa yesterday, Sept. 22, 2016. Senior Airman Scott Fremming brings us the story directly from members of the rescue team.

*The footage used in this video is from a previous training exercise with the 31st and 33rd Rescue Squadrons*
keywords: PILOT RESCUE, pararescure, Okinawa, Marine Corps, Japan, 18th Wing

transcript.text: - Training is the key component that keeps our military
ready for anything at any time.
And it is the constant training of air force units
stationed at Kadena Air Base that allowed them
to be ready at a moment's notice,
when a marine harrier pilot ejected from his aircraft
100 nautical miles east of Okinawa.
- So a marine AV-8 pilot had punched out from his aircraft.
We got notified about within 5-10 minutes later.
And then pretty much had a full-court press at that point
to get our aircraft in the air.
So the HMU did a great job getting us two aircraft
ready to go.
We were wheels up probably about 30 minutes
after the notification.
We had our AFB, our strong troops,
and our cold quest contractors all working
to get the birds up in the air in time.
Went over to the CME ramp, picked up our 31st rescue,
pararescuemen and our crow.
Then we departed out to the northeast to get...
that survivor.
So when we got out there, we found out he was uninjured,
fortunately, so we were able to put one swimmer
in the water to Staff Seargeant Carrol.
He jumped in, got the patient all packaged up,
did an initial assessment to make sure he wasn't too injured
to bring out on this drop.
And then we called the helicopter in
and we strapped him out.
Got him in the helicopter,
did a little more in-depth medical assessment on him
and then brought him to Foster where we
did a patient hand over there.
- Immediately what happened is notification.
We started flying out there...
while en route,
we heard the JASDF over radio,
so they got overhead via fixed wings,
so they were helping provide some situational awareness.
So they dropped...
maybe four to six flairs in the water,
which also had CI marking the area so,
the patient was actually surrounded by like a...
polka dot of green sea dye in the water,
which helped with tracking them down.
- When you train everyday, the real thing is pretty easy.
- It felt like a training mission.
It was like... I don't want to like downplay it like...
but we train.
Usually we train we do like,
day water or night water,
we're shooting guns,
we're doing a scenario so we train just like that,
so yesterday was kind of like the perfect setting
because it was clear, there was no waves,
and we already knew where the guy was,
so usually, we don't know where the guy was,
we're searching for the guy, so we had good
coordinates on where he was,
so as soon as we got on the scene we already...
we knew where he was.
All we had to do was just put the PJ in
and I just hoisted him up.
- Airmen and their JASDF counterparts
keep the keystone of the Pacific Mission ready at all times.
Reporting from Kadena Air Base, Japan,
I'm Senior Airman, Scott Fremming.

pass_reason: release says the footage is from a previous training exercise, so the pictures do not show the real rescue
